newsitem.title: MEXICO: France honours "rebel beauty" of Mexico screen goddess.
newsitem.headline: France honours "rebel beauty" of Mexico screen goddess.

text.p: France bestowed its highest artistic honour on Mexican screen legend Maria Felix on Tuesday, paying tribute to her "rebel beauty" and her 30-year cinema career which included roles with some of the greatest directors of the 1950s and 1960s.
The 82-year-old grande dame swept into the chateau-like French embassy residence for the award dressed in black mink and perfectly made up, looking at least 30 years younger than her age.
Ambassador Bruno Delaye presented the medal recognising Felix's years of residence in Paris, her roles in French films such as "French Can-Can" and her love of France.

Under the glare of television lights and the gaze countless cameramen and reporters in the residence's classical library, Delaye recalled Felix's triumphal first arrival at Paris's Montparnasse station in 1950 at the peak of her fame.

"People said: 'She has the beauty of the devil,' 'She drives men crazy,'" Delaye said. "They say King Farouk of Egypt offered his empire for her ... Charles de Gaulle received her at the Elysee Palace."

Recalling her friendships with French writer Jean Cocteau -- who reputedly said Felix was "so beautiful she causes damage" -- Salvador Dali, Max Ernst, Jean Renoir and Luis Bunuel, Delaye paid tribute to her "eyes of fire and demeanor of a queen" before draping the medal aroud her neck.
The award of Commander of the Order of Arts and Letters was granted to Felix in Mexico at her request. Normally French president Jacques Chirac would have bestowed the honour.

Poised and assured, Felix replied to the assembled guests without a moment's hesitation or a second's pause in her diction: "I dedicate this great honour to Mexican cinema. I also dedicate it to French cinema which gave me the opportunity and also to Mexican culture and Mexican television."
Looking on as she received her award was Octavio Paz, Mexico's Nobel Prize-winning novelist and one of the tiny club of Latin Americans to hold the French honour.
"It makes me very happy first as an old admirer and friend of Maria, secondly as a Mexican and thirdly because she is my companion in this distinction" Paz told Reuters.
While Felix posed for cameras on the marble staircase of the embassy's main halls, one of Mexico's foremost intellectuals, writer Carlos Monsivais, gave his view.

"I think it's just, rather late distinction to a figure who with 57 films crowned an epoch, created a style, launched an image, obtained a nythical niche for herself and established an imperial will in a society in which women were relegated and marginalized", Monsivais told Reuters.
Felix herself said in a magazine interview published at the weekend that she never watched contemporary Mexican films "because I don't like watching bad things."
"Like French cinema and Italian cinema, we are up against the fact that North American cinema occupies 90 percent of the screens all over the world," Monsivais said.
